# Preliminary Analysis

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

<center>**Preliminary Analysis**</center>

:::

Based upon the rate expressions, the instantaneous selectivity is favored by a high concentration of A and a low concentration of B, equation (5). Assuming negligible temperature effects, starting the process with all of the A in the reactor keeps the concentration of A a large as possible at all times, and adding the B slowly can keep its concentration as low as desired. Both of those factors favor high selectivity for D over U.

$$
S_{D/U,inst} = \frac{r_D}{r_U} = \frac{r_1}{r_2} = \frac{k_D}{k_U} \frac{C_A}{C_B} \tag{5}
$$

Presumably the reactions are not extremely fast because the reactor is allowed to operate in batch mode after semi-batch processing ends. As such, the final conversion of B is expected to decrease the longer the addition time because reagent added near the end of semi-batch processing will have less time to react during the batch stage.

As the addition time increases, the selectivity for D over U is expected to increase because the slower the addition of B, the lower its concentration and the higher the selectivity. Yield is affected by both conversion and selectivity, so a trade-off is expected. The decrease in conversion with semi-batch processing time will tend to decrease the yield while the increase in selectivity will tend to increase it. Quantitative analysis is necessary to determine how the yield will vary with semi-batch processing time.

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Click Here to See What an Expert Might be Thinking at this Point

I'm going to need to solve the SBSTR Design equations to complete this assignment, so I'll start by defining a SBSTR model function. To do that I'll need to 

* generate and simplify the design equations, 
* identify the SBSTR model variables I'll get by solving them, 
* identify any additional computable unknowns they contain and write the equations for calculating them,
* identify any non-computable unknows that will need to be passed to the BSTR model function as arguments, and
* determine the type of equation solver that I'll need and what input it will require.

Mole balances are always needed, and I prefer to write a mole balance for every reagent in the system other than solvent. The general SBSTR mole balance is given in @eq-sbstr_mole_bal. Two reactions take place in this system, so the summation expands to two terms. The inlet molar flow rates of A, D, and U are all equal to zero. The only difference when there is a second phase of operation is that the inlet molar flow rate of reagent B is also equal to zero.

$$
\frac{dn_i}{dt} = \dot n_{i,in} + V \sum_j \nu_{i,j}r_j \Rightarrow \frac{dn_i}{dt} = \dot n_{i,in} + \nu_{i,1} V r_1 + \nu_{i,2} V r_2
$$

The reactor is not isothermal, so the mole balances cannot be solved independently of an energy balance. The general energy balance for an SBSTR is given in @eq-sbstr_energy_bal. The narrative provides a volumetric heat capacity that applies to solutions of A and B. Presumably this heat capacity is essentially equal to that of the solvent, so it can be used for both the reacting fluid and the feed stream, replacing the summations over molar heat capacities. The heat capacity is constant, so it can be taken outside of the integral, and the resulting trivial integral can be evaluated. The reactor is adiabatic, so $\dot{Q}$ is equal to zero and apart from agitation, no work is being done so $\dot{W}$ is neglibible. The reacting fluid is a liquid, so the pressure is constant and its time derivative is zero. Finally, two reactions are taking place, so the final summation expands to two terms. The only differences when there is a second phase of operation are that the $\frac{dV}{dt}$ term and the inlet volumetric flow rate are equal to zero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cancelto{V \breve{C}_p}{\sum_i \left( n_i \hat C_{p,i}\right)}  \frac{dT}{dt} &-V\cancelto{0}{\frac{dP}{dt}} - P\frac{dV}{dt} = \cancelto{0}{\dot Q} - \cancelto{0}{\dot W} \\&- \cancelto{\dot{V}_{in} \breve{C}_p \left( T - T_{in} \right)}{\sum_i \dot n_{i,in} \int_{T_{in}}^T \hat C_{p,i}dT}  - V\cancelto{\left(r_1 \Delta H_1 + r_2 \Delta H_2\right)}{\sum_j r_j \Delta H_j}
\end{aligned}
$$

Being an adiabatic reactor, there isn't an exchange fluid, so an exchange fluid energy balance is not needed. To this point, though, there are five ODE design equations, but they contain six dependent variables. So I either need to eliminate a dependent variable or add a design equation. I'll do the latter. Assuming the reacting fluid is an ideal mixture, the rate of change of the reacting fluid volume will equal the volumetric feed rate.

:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="pdf"}

# SBSTR Model Function

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

<center>**SBSTR Model Function**</center>

:::

[SBSTR Design Equations]{.underline}

$$
\frac{dn_A}{dt} = -r_1V \tag{6}
$$

$$
\frac{dn_B}{dt} = \dot{n}_{B,in} -\left(r_1 + 2 r_2\right)V \tag{7}
$$

$$
\frac{dn_D}{dt} = r_1V \tag{8}
$$

$$
\frac{dn_U}{dt} = r_2V \tag{9}
$$

$$
V \breve{C}_p \frac{dT}{dt} - P\frac{dV}{dt} = -\dot{V}_{in}\breve{C}_p \left(T - T_{in} \right)  - r_1V \Delta H_1 - r_2V \Delta H_2 \tag{10}
$$

$$
\frac{dV}{dt} = \dot{V}_{in} \tag{11}
$$

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Click Here to See What an Expert Might be Thinking at this Point

The design equations are IVODEs, so they will be solved to find corresponding sets of values of the independent ($t$) and dependent ($n_A$, $n_B$, $n_D$, $n_U$, $T$, and $V$) variables. To do that any additional unknowns must first be calculated. Reviewing the design equations variable-by-variable, it is seen that the rates, inlet molar flow of B, and inlet volumetric flow rate are additional unknowns.

The rates can be calculated using the rate expressions provided in the assignment narrative. That introduces the rate coefficients and the concentrations of A and B as additional unknowns. The rate coefficients can be computed using the Arrhenius expression and the concentrations using their defining equations. The inlet molar flow rate of B can be calculated from the inlet volumetric flow rate and the inlet concentration of B, and the inlet volumetric flow rate from the volume of B to be added and the time over which it will be added.

The time over which B will be added cannot be computed. It is a parameter that will need to be provided at the time the equations are being solved.

:::

:::

[SBSTR Model Variables]{.underline}: $\underline{t}$, $\underline{n}_A$, $\underline{n}_B$, $\underline{n}_D$, $\underline{n}_U$, $\underline{T}$, and $\underline{V}$

[Additional Computable Unknowns]{.underline}: $r_1$, $r_2$, $k_1$, $k_2$, $C_A$, $C_B$, $\dot{n}_{B,in}$, and $\dot{V}_{in}$

$$
k_i = k_{0,i} \exp{\left(\frac{-E_i}{RT}\right)} \qquad i = 1 \text{ and } 2 \tag{12}
$$

$$
C_i = \frac{n_i}{V} \qquad i = A \text{ and } B \tag{13}
$$

$$
\dot{n}_{B,in} = \dot{V}_{in}C_{B,in} \tag{14}
$$

$$
\begin{matrix}
\dot{V}_{in} = \frac{V_B}{t_1}; \qquad \text{stage 1}\\[0.5em]
\dot{V}_{in} = 0; \qquad \text{stage 2}
\end{matrix} \tag {15}
$$

[Uncomputable Unknowns (Received as Arguments)]{.underline}: $t_1$

If a single SBSTR derivatives is used, it needs $t_1$ and the stage number  (see equation (15)), so the SBSTR model function must make them available as global variables. Alternatively separate derivatives functions could be written for each stage, in which case global variables would not be needed.

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Click Here to See What an Expert Might be Thinking at this Point

The design equations are IVODEs and to solve numerically them I must provide initial values, a stopping criterion, and a derivatives function.I can define $t=0$ to be the time when the flow of reagent B into the reactor begins. The reacting fluid temperature and volume at that time are known. Only reagent A is present in the reactor, and its molar amount can be calculated using the known initial volume and initial concentration of A. The first stage of operation ends when the flow of reagent B ends at $t_{1}$.

The second stage begins immediately. Consequently the initial values are equal to the final values from the first stage, and they will be known after the design equations have been solved for the first stage. The second stage ends after 8 h of operation.

If the same derivatives function is used for both stages, the stage number and current value of $t_1$ will be available to it as global variables. It will receive the reactor model variables and must return the derivatives of the dependent variables with respect to the independent variable, $t$. Except for the energy balance, each of the design equations is written as a derivatives expression. To calculate the derivative of the temperature with respect to time, equation (10) can be substituted in the energy balance, which then can be solved for $\frac{dT}{dt}$.

:::

:::

[IVODE Solver Requirements]{.underline}

1. Stage 1

    a. Initial values
$$
t_{iv,1} = t_1 \tag{16}
$$
$$
n_{A,iv,1} = n_{A,0} = C_{A,0}V_A \tag{17}
$$
$$
n_{i,iv,1} = 0 \qquad i = B, D, \text{ and } U \tag{18}
$$
$$
T_{iv,1} = T_0 \tag{19}
$$
$$
V_{iv,1} = V_A \tag{20}
$$
    b. Stopping criterion
$$
t = t_1 \tag{21}
$$

2. Stage 2

    a. Initial values
$$
t_{iv,2} = t_1 \tag{22}
$$
$$
n_{i,iv,2} = n_i \big|_{t=t_1} \qquad i = A, B, D, \text{ and } U \tag{23}
$$
$$
T_{iv,2} = T \big|_{t=t_1} \tag{24}
$$
$$
V_{iv,2} = V \big|_{t=t_1} \tag{25}
$$
    b. Stopping criterion
$$
t = t_f \tag{26}
$$

3. (both stages) SBSTR derivatives function that
    a. receives the reactor model variables at the start of an integration step
    b. can access the current value of $t_1$ and the stage number
    c. calculates the additional unknowns using equations (3), (4), and (12) - (15)
    d. evaluates and returns the SBSTR design equation SBSTR derivatives using equations (6) - (11)

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="pdf"}

To facilitate making $t_1$ and the stage number available to the SBSTR derivatives function, the global variables, `g_t1` and `g_stage`, are declared and set to `nan` initially. Then the SBSTR model and SBSTR derivatives functions are added to `ex_8_4_2`.

```matlab
    % define a global variables for the current value of t1 and the current protocol stage
    g_t1 = nan;
    g_stage = -1;

    % SBSTR reactor function
    function [t, nA, nB, nD, nU, T, V] = sbstr_model_variables(t1)
        % make t1 available to the derivatives function
        g_t1 = t1;

        % set the current operational protocol stage;
        g_stage = 1;

        % set the initial values
        ind_0 = 0;
        dep_0 = [nA_0, 0, 0, 0, T_0, V_A];

        % set the stopping criterion
        stopVar = 0;
        stopVal = t1;

        % solve the IVODE design equations
        odes_are_stiff = false;
        [t1, dep1, success, message] = solve_ivodes(ind_0, dep_0, stopVar...
            , stopVal, @sbstr_derivatives, odes_are_stiff);
        
        % check for solver issues
        if ~success
            disp('')
            disp(["SBSTR model stage 1 issue: ", message])
            disp('Press any key to continue or CTRL-C to exit')
            pause
        end
        
        % repeat for the second stage
        g_stage = 2;
        ind_0 = t1(end);
        dep_0 = [dep1(end,1), dep1(end,2), dep1(end,3), dep1(end,4)...
            , dep1(end,5), dep1(end,6)];
        stopVal = tf;
        [t2, dep2, success, message] = solve_ivodes(ind_0, dep_0, stopVar...
            , stopVal, @sbstr_derivatives, odes_are_stiff);
        if ~success
            disp('')
            disp(["SBSTR model stage 2 issue: ", message])
            disp('Press any key to continue or CTRL-C to exit')
            pause
        end
        
        % concatenate the stages
        t = [t1; t2];
        nA = [dep1(:,1); dep2(:,1)];
        nB = [dep1(:,2); dep2(:,2)];
        nD = [dep1(:,3); dep2(:,3)];
        nU = [dep1(:,4); dep2(:,4)];
        T = [dep1(:,5); dep2(:,5)];
        V = [dep1(:,6); dep2(:,6)];
    end

    % SBSTR derivatives function
    function ddt = sbstr_derivatives(~, dep)
        % extract the dependent variables
        nA = dep(1);
        nB = dep(2);
        T = dep(5);
        V = dep(6);

        % calculate the additional unknowns
        if g_stage == 1
            Vdot_in = V_B/g_t1;
        else
            Vdot_in = 0.0;
        end
        k_1 = k0_1*exp(-E_1/Re/T);
        k_2 = k0_2*exp(-E_2/Re/T);
        CA = nA/V;
        CB = nB/V;
        r_1 = k_1*CA*CB;
        r_2 = k_2*CB^2;
        nDotB_in = Vdot_in*CB_in;

        % evaluate the derivatives
        dnAdt = -V*r_1;
        dnBdt = nDotB_in - V*(r_1 + 2*r_2);
        dnDdt = V*r_1;
        dnUdt = V*r_2;
        dTdt = (-Vdot_in*Cp*(T - T_in) - V*r_1*dH_1 - V*r_2*dH_2...
            + P*Vdot_in*Re/Rw)/(V*Cp);
        dVdt = Vdot_in;

        % return the derivatives as a column vector
        ddt = [dnAdt; dnBdt; dnDdt; dnUdt; dTdt; dVdt];
    end
```

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

# Items of Interest Function

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

<center>**Items of Interest Function**</center>

:::

1. Loop through the specified values of $t_1$
    a. Call the SBSTR reactor model function to get $\underline{t}$, $\underline{n}_A$, $\underline{n}_B$, $\underline{n}_D$, $\underline{n}_U$, $\underline{T}$, and $\underline{V}$
    b. Calculate and save the corresponding conversion, selectivity, and yield
$$
f_B = \frac{V_BC_{B,in} - \underline{n}_B\big|_{t_f}}{V_BC_{B,in}} \tag{27}
$$
$$
S_{D/U} = \frac{\underline{n}_D\big|_{t_f}}{\underline{n}_U\big|_{t_f}} \tag{28}
$$
$$
Y_{D/B} = \frac{\underline{n}_D\big|_{t_f}}{V_BC_{B,in}} \tag{29}
$$
2. Tabulate, show, and save the results

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="pdf"}

To complete `ex_8_4_2`, the items of interest function was added along with a line of code to call it and perform the calculations.

```matlab
    % items of interest function
    function items_of_interest()
        % allocate storage for the results
        nParams = length(t1_range);
        f_B = ones(1, nParams)*nan;
        S_DU = ones(1, nParams)*nan;
        Y_DB = ones(1, nParams)*nan;

        % loop through the t1 values
        for i = 1:nParams
            % solve the design equations
            [~, ~, nB, nD, nU, ~, ~] = sbstr_model_variables(t1_range(i));

            % calculate and save the quantities of interest
            f_B(i) = 100*(V_B*CB_in - nB(end))/(V_B*CB_in);
            S_DU(i) = nD(end)/nU(end);
            Y_DB(i) = 100*nD(end)/(V_B*CB_in);
        end
        
        % tabulate, show and save the results
        resultsTable = table(t1_range.', f_B.', S_DU.', Y_DB.');
        resultsTable.Properties.VariableNames = ["Stage 1 Duration (h)",...
            "Conversion (%)", "Selectivity D/U", "Yield D-B (%)"];
        disp('')
        disp(resultsTable)
        disp('')
        writetable(resultsTable, 'ex_8_4_2_results.csv')
    end

    % perform the calculations
    items_of_interest()
end
```

:::

<center>**Implementation of the Calculations.**</center>

 Computer code to perform the calculations can be written using a variety of programming languages and environments, and the actual code can be structured in a variety of ways. Referring to the preceding assignment summary, computational strategy and formulation of the equations, here are the essential things it must do.

1. Make the given and known constants available wherever they are needed
2. Define the derivatives function.
3. Define the initial values and stopping criterion for the first stage
4. Make the duration of the first stage available to the derivatives function
5. Call an IVODE solver
	a. pass the initial values and stopping criterion for the first stage and the derivatives function as arguments, and
	b. receive the reactor model variables for the first stage.
6. Repeat steps 3 through 5 for the second stage.
7. Calculate the quantities of interest.

One way to structure the code, based on the preceding workup, is to write a single master function for the assignment. Within it declare the given constants as global constants, declare the global variables to make $%$t_1$ and the current stage number available to the derivatives function, and define the BSTR model function, the BSTR derivatives function, and the items of interest function. Then call the items of interest function.

# Discussion

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

<center>**Discussion**</center>

:::

@tbl-ch8_ex2_results shows that the conversion of B decreases as its addition gets spread over longer times. This is reasonable because as noted in the preliminary analysis, the later in the process that the B is added, the less time it has to react. Separate calculations show that if the reaction is run in a batch reactor the conversion is 85.7% with a selectivity for D over U of 2.88 and a yield of D from B of 50.6%.

As previously noted, adding the B to A over time keeps the concentration of A as large as possible at all times and keeps the concentration of B lower than if it was all added at the start. The expression for the instantaneous selectivity for D over U for these reactions, equation (5), suggests that this should result in greater selectivity, and indeed, @tbl-ch8_ex2_results shows that the slower the B is added (i. e. the longer the time during which it is added), the greater the selectivity for D over U.

However, while the selectivity is increasing, the conversion of B is decreasing. As a consequence, the yield of D from B is nearly constant at approximately 50%, passing through a weak maximum when B is added over 3 h. The processing time in all cases is the same, 8 h. Hence, the operating costs, are basically the same. The net rate of production of D is essentially the same, too, because the yield of D is effectively constant.

In effect, the same amount of B is converted to D in all four cases, but as the addition time increases, the amount of B converted to U decreases while the amount of unreacted B increases. Comparing batch processing to semi-batch processing where the B is added during the first 7 h of the 8 h process, the same amount of D is produced at the same net rate. The difference is that in semi-batch mode there is more unreacted B while in batch mode there is more undesired U.

Semi-batch processing where the B is added during the first 7 h of the 8 h process has an advantage over batch processing in two scenarios. First, if reagent B is easily and inexpensively separable from the product mixture, not converting it to U, but instead recovering it and re-using it in a subsequent semi-batch run mitigates the low conversion.

The other scenario is when U is a valueless hazardous waste. The disposal of such a waste can add significantly to the cost of the process, thereby decreasing profits. In this scenario, even if the unconverted B cannot be separated and re-used, the cost of wasting reagent B (i. e. low conversion) may be more than offset by significantly lower expenses associated with disposal of U (because less U is generated).

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="pdf"}

# Summary

:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}

<center>**Summary**</center>

:::

@tbl-ch8_ex2_results summarizes the effect of varying the rate of addition of B upon conversion, selectivity and yield. As the rate of addition increases, the conversion increases and the selectivity decreases with the yield remaining approximately constant.

As the semi-batch processing time is increased, holding the total processing time constant, the conversion of B decreases from 84.3 to 67.6%, the selectivity for D over U increases from 3.17 to 5.33, and the yield of D is close to constant at 50%. In consequence, as the semi-batch processing time increases the amount of undesired product decreases and the amount of unreacted B increases.
